title: The Boy Who Was Hugged by a Soldier
author: Daniel Kahneman
wiifm: Every lead you price, every advert you approve and every client file you judge in thirty seconds runs on mental machinery you never chose and cannot switch off. This week is about that operating system, and we start with the man who mapped it. You will follow Daniel Kahneman from occupied Paris to the Israeli army, into one of the great intellectual friendships of the twentieth century, and out the other side to a Nobel Prize. By the end you will know when to trust your gut, and exactly when not to.

b: Daniel Kahneman was born in Tel Aviv in March 1934, while his mother was visiting family, but he grew up in Paris. His parents were Lithuanian Jews who had settled in France, and his father was head of research at a chemical company. When the Germans occupied Paris in 1940, the boy was six.

By late 1941 Jews in Paris lived under a curfew, and from 1942 they had to wear the yellow star. One evening Daniel had stayed late at a Christian friend's house and was walking home with his sweater turned inside out so the star would not show. The street was empty. Then a German soldier appeared in the black uniform of the SS, the uniform he had been told to fear most.

The soldier beckoned him over, picked him up and hugged him. Then he put him down, opened his wallet, showed him a photograph of a little boy and gave him some money. The child went home, Kahneman wrote decades later, more certain than ever that his mother was right: people were endlessly complicated and interesting.

The family's war got far worse. His father was caught in a mass roundup and held at the Drancy camp, then released after about six weeks, apparently through his employer's intervention. The family fled south and hid. His father died of untreated diabetes in 1944, a few weeks before the Allied landings in Normandy. In 1948 Daniel, his mother and his sister reached Palestine, shortly before the State of Israel was declared.

Hold on to that soldier. A lifetime of research was about to show that the human mind is neither a cold calculator nor a wicked one. It is a machine that produces judgements quickly, coherently and often wrongly, and the person running it rarely notices.
ch.cap: On a curfew street, an SS soldier hugs a boy

ch.h: The interview that beat the officers
b: Kahneman studied psychology and mathematics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and in 1954 he was drafted into the Israel Defence Forces. At twenty-one he was handed a remarkable job: fix the way the army assessed its recruits.

The existing method was an interview in which officers formed a general impression of each young man. Kahneman replaced it with something deliberately dull. Interviewers asked factual questions about six traits, such as responsibility and sociability, scored each one separately and only then added the scores together. The interviewers hated it and complained they had been turned into robots. So he let them close their eyes at the end and give one intuitive overall rating as well.

The structured scores predicted later performance far better than the old impressions had. And the intuitive rating, made after the facts had been gathered, turned out to be useful too. It was an early version of a lesson he taught for the rest of his life: intuition is worth most when it comes last, after disciplined evidence, not first. The army went on using a version of his interview for decades.

Around the same time he watched officer candidates in a leaderless team exercise, struggling to get a log over a wall. He and his colleagues felt completely confident about who would make a good leader. Months later the reports from officer school arrived, and their predictions turned out to be barely better than chance. Then the next batch of candidates arrived, and they felt exactly as confident as before. He called this the illusion of validity. Knowing that you are often wrong in general does almost nothing to stop you feeling right in particular.
ch.cap: Scoring recruits trait by trait while cadets haul a log

b: After a doctorate at Berkeley, finished in 1961, Kahneman went home to teach at the Hebrew University. In the mid-1960s he was lecturing flight instructors in the Israeli air force, explaining that rewarding good performance works better than punishing mistakes.

A senior instructor objected. Whenever he praised a cadet for a beautiful manoeuvre, the next attempt was usually worse. Whenever he shouted at a cadet for a bad one, the next was usually better. So please do not tell us that reward works, he said. We have seen the opposite.

Kahneman realised the instructor was describing something real and explaining it wrongly. Every performance contains luck. An exceptionally good attempt was probably helped by luck, so the next one will tend to drift back towards average whatever the instructor says. An exceptionally bad one will tend to improve on its own. This is regression to the mean, and the instructor had spent years crediting his shouting for what statistics would have done anyway.

It became one of the central ideas of the book. Our minds hunt for causes and stories and are poor at seeing chance. A sales team has a record month, nothing changes, and the next month is merely good. Someone gets blamed. Often nobody did anything at all.
ch.cap: A flight instructor shouts; the scores drift back to average

ch.h: Two men in a seminar room
b: In the spring of 1969 Kahneman invited a younger colleague, Amos Tversky, to speak to his seminar. Tversky was brilliant, combative and famously quick, a former paratrooper who had come back from Michigan trained in mathematical models of choice. He presented research suggesting that people are roughly sensible intuitive statisticians. Kahneman, who had spent years watching instructors and officers misread evidence, told him he did not believe a word of it.

Instead of falling out, they started having lunch. Then they started spending whole days together, talking and laughing in a closed room, writing papers one sentence at a time. Their method was to invent questions, answer them with their own gut, and treat their own mistakes as data. If two experts in statistics got it wrong intuitively, ordinary people surely would.

They were opposites. Kahneman was a worrier, gloomy and self-doubting, forever suspecting he was wrong. Tversky was an optimist who rarely doubted anything and was famous for falling asleep the moment a dull talk began. Colleagues said that the two of them together were sharper than either apart, and they agreed. They tossed a coin to decide whose name would come first on their papers, then alternated. For more than a decade it was nearly impossible to say which idea belonged to whom, and they liked it that way.

Their first joint paper, in 1971, was called Belief in the Law of Small Numbers. It showed that even trained researchers trust tiny samples far too much. Then, in 1974, came a paper in the journal Science that made them famous: Judgment under Uncertainty, Heuristics and Biases. Its argument was simple and devastating. When faced with a hard question, the mind quietly swaps in an easier one and answers that instead, and the swap leaves predictable fingerprints.
ch.cap: Kahneman and Tversky toss a coin for first billing

ch.h: A wheel of fortune and a woman called Linda
b: The fingerprints had names. One was anchoring. In one experiment the pair spun a wheel of fortune, rigged to stop at either ten or sixty-five, in front of their subjects, then asked what percentage of African nations were in the United Nations. People who had seen ten guessed around twenty-five per cent. People who had seen sixty-five guessed around forty-five. A number everyone knew to be random had dragged their estimates with it.

Another was availability. We judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid, recent or heavily reported events feel more likely than they are. A third was representativeness, judging probability by how well something fits a stereotype. In a famous 1983 study they described Linda, a bright, outspoken philosophy graduate concerned with social justice, and asked whether it was more probable that she was a bank teller, or a bank teller active in the feminist movement. Most people chose the second, even though it cannot be more likely than the first, because it is a narrower version of it.

In the 2011 book Kahneman wrapped all of this in a single picture, borrowing labels from the psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West. System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless: it reads faces, finishes sentences and jumps to conclusions. System 2 is slow, deliberate and lazy: it does long division and checks arguments, but only when forced. Most of the time System 2 simply endorses whatever System 1 hands it. He was careful to say these are characters in a story, not places in the brain.
ch.cap: A rigged wheel stops at sixty-five and drags the guesses

b: Economics in the 1970s assumed that people choose by weighing final states of wealth. Kahneman and Tversky noticed that nobody actually thinks this way. We think about changes from where we stand now, gains and losses, and we feel them unequally. Their 1979 paper, Prospect Theory, published in the journal Econometrica, set this out formally and became one of the most cited papers in the history of economics.

The heart of it is loss aversion. Offer most people a coin toss where they lose one hundred pounds on tails, and they will want to win around two hundred on heads before they accept. Losing hurts roughly twice as much as winning pleases. The same logic explains why people cling to failing shares, why a price framed as a discount sells better than the same price framed as a surcharge, and why a ninety per cent survival rate sounds kinder than a ten per cent death rate, even to doctors.

Their friendship did not survive its success intact. In 1978 Tversky went to Stanford and Kahneman, with his second wife the psychologist Anne Treisman, to the University of British Columbia. The world treated Tversky as the senior partner, and Kahneman felt it keenly. They drifted, and were only partly reconciled when Tversky was diagnosed with melanoma. He died in 1996, aged fifty-nine. In 2002 Kahneman received the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics. He said publicly that it was a joint prize, and that Amos should have been there.
ch.cap: At the Nobel podium, an empty chair for Amos

b: Later in his career Kahneman turned to happiness, and found that even here we are split. The experiencing self lives moment to moment. The remembering self keeps score and makes the decisions. They disagree. In studies of colonoscopy patients run with the physician Donald Redelmeier from the 1990s, patients' memories of pain depended mostly on the worst moment and the final moments, and hardly at all on how long the procedure lasted. He called it the peak-end rule. In a later trial, adding a few minutes of milder discomfort at the end made people remember the whole thing as less unpleasant.

He also told a story against himself. In the 1970s he led a team writing a decision-making curriculum for Israeli high schools. He asked everyone to estimate how long it would take, and the answers clustered around two years. Then he asked the curriculum expert on the team how long similar projects had taken. After a pause the man admitted that many never finished, and the rest took seven to ten years. They carried on anyway. It took eight years, and the curriculum was barely used.

Notice what happened in that room. The expert had the outside information all along. He simply had not consulted it until asked, because the plan in front of him felt so specific and so reasonable. Kahneman did not blame him. He blamed the way the mind treats a vivid case. We build a story of how our project will unfold, step by step, and the story contains no illness, no resignation, no delayed supplier. Real projects contain all three.

Kahneman called this the planning fallacy, and the cure is what he called the outside view. Before you trust your own detailed plan, ask how long things like it usually take for people like you. The inside view is full of specific, hopeful detail. The outside view is boring and usually right.
ch.cap: The team guesses two years; the expert says seven

ch.h: The train wreck he saw coming
b: Thinking, Fast and Slow was published in 2011, when Kahneman was seventy-seven, and became a worldwide bestseller. But one chapter has aged badly, and he said so himself.

Chapter four leaned on priming studies: claims that reading words about old age makes people walk more slowly afterwards, or that pictures of money make them more selfish. Kahneman wrote that disbelief was not an option. Within a year, other laboratories were failing to reproduce several of these results. In 2012 he wrote an open letter to priming researchers warning of a train wreck looming and urging them to replicate each other's work.

In 2017 the psychologists Ulrich Schimmack and Moritz Heene, with Kulia Kesavan, analysed the studies behind that chapter and argued they were too small to be trusted. Kahneman replied publicly that he had placed too much faith in underpowered studies, and that readers should not rely on the priming chapter. It was a rare and graceful act, and fitting: the man who taught the world about overconfidence admitted to his own.

The core of the book stands on firmer ground. Anchoring, loss aversion, framing and the planning fallacy have been reproduced many times, though the size of some effects is debated. The lesson is to hold the fast system's confident stories, including the ones in this book, a little more loosely.
ch.cap: Kahneman writes his warning as a train nears the gap

b: Kahneman died in March 2024, aged ninety. He had spent his last decades at Princeton and wrote one more book, Noise, about the random scatter in professional judgement. Even late in life he remained cheerful about one thing: he did not think his own biases had improved much. Knowing about System 1 does not tame it.

What does work, he argued, is designing the environment. Score candidates on separate traits before forming an overall view, as he did for the army at twenty-one. Ask for the base rate before the story. Write down predictions so hindsight cannot rewrite them. Run a premortem, an idea from the psychologist Gary Klein, in which the team imagines the project has failed a year from now and writes the history of the failure.

And trust intuition only where it has earned trust: in a regular environment, with lots of practice and quick, honest feedback. A nurse reading a deteriorating patient, a firefighter sensing a floor about to go. Not a stock picker, and not a recruiter judging a stranger in an interview.

The six-year-old in Paris learned that people are complicated. The old man in Princeton had shown exactly how. We are fast, fluent storytellers, and the stories feel true. The discipline is to slow down at the moments that matter, and check.
ch.cap: The old professor remembers the soldier and the boy

take: Kahneman's army interview scored separate traits before allowing an overall feeling. Use the same order when hiring, reviewing a client file or judging a supplier: gather structured evidence, then let intuition have its say.
The illusion of validity means you can feel certain while being barely better than chance. When you feel very sure about a person or a deal, treat that as a prompt to check, not as proof.
Exceptional months are usually followed by ordinary ones. Before crediting or blaming anyone for a swing in results, ask whether it would have happened anyway.
The first number in the room drags every estimate after it. Set your own figure before you hear the other side's, and be the one who names the number first in a negotiation.
People feel a loss about twice as sharply as an equal gain. Frame offers as what the customer keeps or avoids losing, and watch for your own refusal to cut a failing campaign.
Before trusting your plan's timeline, ask how long similar projects usually take. Add the base rate to your own detailed hopes and expect overruns.
The remembering self judges an experience by its peak and its end. Make the last contact a customer has with you the best one.
Even Kahneman's priming chapter failed to replicate, and he said so. Check the evidence behind a striking claim before building a strategy on it.
recall: System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive, and produces impressions and conclusions without effort. System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful, and usually just endorses what System 1 suggests. Kahneman presented them as useful characters, not literal brain regions.
What did the flight instructor get wrong?

He believed shouting improved cadets and praise made them worse. In fact performance naturally drifts back towards average after an unusually good or bad attempt. He was seeing regression to the mean and mistaking it for the effect of his own feedback.

It is the finding, central to prospect theory in 1979, that losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains please. It explains why people refuse fair bets, cling to losing investments and respond strongly to how a choice is framed.
What is the planning fallacy and its cure?

It is our tendency to underestimate how long and how much a project will take by focusing on our specific plan. Kahneman's own curriculum team expected two years and took eight. The cure is the outside view: check how similar projects have actually gone.
Which part of the book did Kahneman himself disown?

The chapter on social priming, such as the idea that words about old age make people walk slowly. Many of those studies failed to replicate, and in 2017 he admitted he had placed too much faith in underpowered studies.
note: Biographical details come mainly from Kahneman's Nobel autobiography of 2002 and Michael Lewis's The Undoing Project. The SS soldier story is Kahneman's own recollection. The 1974 Science paper, 1979 prospect theory paper and 1983 Linda study are documented. The priming chapter has largely failed to replicate, as Kahneman acknowledged in 2017; anchoring, framing and loss aversion are broadly robust, though effect sizes are debated.
words: A mental shortcut or rule of thumb that gives a quick answer without full analysis.
Kahneman and Tversky's 1974 paper showed that heuristics such as anchoring and availability leave predictable errors in our judgements.
The tendency of an unusually extreme result to be followed by one closer to average, simply because luck evens out.
The flight instructor credited his shouting for improvements that regression to the mean would have produced anyway.
The way an initial number, even a random one, drags later estimates towards it.
Subjects who saw a rigged wheel stop at sixty-five guessed far more African nations were in the United Nations than those who saw ten.
The error of judging two things happening together as more likely than one of them alone.
Most people said Linda was more likely to be a feminist bank teller than a bank teller, which is logically impossible.
Describes a study with too few participants to detect a real effect reliably, so its results may be flukes.
Kahneman admitted he had trusted underpowered priming studies, and told readers not to rely on that chapter.
stories: Paris, around 1942. A small Jewish boy is walking home after curfew with his sweater turned inside out to hide his yellow star. A soldier in the black SS uniform, the one he has been taught to fear most, beckons him over. The boy is terrified. The soldier picks him up and hugs him, shows him a photograph of his own little son, and gives him some money. The boy was Daniel Kahneman, and he went home sure his mother was right: people are endlessly complicated. He spent the rest of his life proving exactly how.
The instructor who believed in shouting

In the 1960s Kahneman told Israeli air force instructors that praise works better than punishment. A senior instructor pushed back. Every time he praised a cadet for a brilliant manoeuvre, the next one was worse. Every time he screamed at a cadet for a bad one, the next was better. Kahneman realised the man had seen something real and explained it wrongly. A brilliant attempt is partly luck, so the next one drifts back to average whatever you say. The instructor had spent years crediting his own shouting for plain statistics. That is regression to the mean.
The textbook that took eight years

In the 1970s Kahneman led a team writing a decision-making course for Israeli schools. He asked everyone how long it would take. The answers clustered around two years. Then he asked the curriculum expert how long similar projects usually took. After a long pause the man admitted many never finished, and the rest took seven to ten years. Everyone carried on regardless. It took eight years and was barely used. The expert had the answer all along and never thought to look. Kahneman called it the planning fallacy, and the cure is to ask how long things like this normally take.
biz: Stop reacting to one good week

Regression to the mean is everywhere in paid search. A week of cheap leads on Google or Bing is often luck, and so is a bad one. Before anyone changes bids or blames a landing page, agree a simple rule with whoever runs the ad accounts: judge cost per qualified lead on a rolling four-week view against the previous quarter, and only act when it moves outside that normal range. This week, pull twelve weeks of cost per lead and lead-to-application rate, plot the spread, and write down what counts as a genuine shift rather than noise.
Facts first, gut last on every file

Kahneman beat the army's officers by scoring separate traits before any overall impression. Do the same with Debt Support Direct and HomeownersLoan enquiries. Build a short structured checklist the adviser completes before forming a view: income stability, priority debts, existing secured borrowing, and the FCA's vulnerability drivers of health, life events, resilience and capability from its FG21/1 guidance. Only then record a gut note. It protects clients in distress from snap judgements on a busy afternoon. Measure how often the checklist flags vulnerability the first impression missed.
connects: Tetlock's superforecasters succeed by starting from the base rate, the same outside view Kahneman used against the planning fallacy.
Gawande's checklists, like Kahneman's army interview, show that a dull structured routine beats confident expert intuition.
Munger's talk on the psychology of human misjudgement catalogues many of the same biases, from anchoring to overconfidence, for practical decision-makers.
recap:
In Paris during the war, a small Jewish boy hurried home after curfew with his sweater turned inside out to hide his yellow star. A soldier in the black uniform of the SS stopped him, picked him up and hugged him, showed him a photograph of his own son, and gave him money. The boy was Daniel Kahneman, and he never forgot that people are endlessly complicated. His father died before liberation, the family reached Palestine in nineteen forty eight, and Kahneman became a psychologist.

At twenty one, in the Israeli army, he replaced vague officer interviews with a dull method: score six separate traits, add them up, and only then allow a gut feeling. It predicted far better. That is the first big idea. Intuition is most useful when it comes last, after the evidence, not first.

Later he watched an air force instructor insist that shouting improved cadets and praise made them worse. Kahneman saw the real cause. Extreme performances are partly luck, so the next attempt drifts back towards average whatever anyone says. That is regression to the mean, the second idea, and it means we constantly credit and blame people for chance.

In nineteen sixty nine he met Amos Tversky, a brilliant former paratrooper, and the two became one of the great partnerships in science. They tested their own gut answers and found the fingerprints of mental shortcuts. A random number on a spinning wheel dragged people's estimates. Vivid examples felt more common than they were. A woman called Linda seemed more likely to be a feminist bank teller than simply a bank teller, which is impossible. The third idea is that the mind quietly swaps a hard question for an easy one, and the fast, automatic part of thinking, System one, hands its answer to a lazy System two that usually signs it off.

Their prospect theory added the fourth idea. Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains please, which explains clinging to failing shares and the power of how a choice is framed. Tversky died in nineteen ninety six. When Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in two thousand and two, he said Amos should have been there.

The fifth idea is humility. Plans ignore how long such projects usually take, so ask for the base rate first. And when his own chapter on priming failed to replicate, Kahneman said so in public.

He died in twenty twenty four, aged ninety, still convinced his own biases had barely improved. You cannot switch the fast mind off. You can only build habits that make you slow down when it matters.

The line to remember: feeling certain is not the same as being right.
